parole.significato: asteroid (naturally occurring solid object, which is smaller than a planet and is not a comet, that orbits a star)
parole.testo: Internationalism, based on English asteroid, probably coined as a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀστεροειδής (asteroeidḗs, “starlike”).
From English atom, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).
From English endocrine, from Ancient Greek ἔνδον (éndon, “inner; internal”) + Ancient Greek κρίνω (krínō, “to separate”).
Borrowed from English ethnography, from Ancient Greek ἔθνος (éthnos, “people, nation”) + γράφω (gráphō, “write, draw”). With -gráfia ending.
From English pheromone, from Ancient Greek φέρω (phérō, “I bring, bear, carry”).

parole.significato: glucose (a simple monosaccharide (sugar) with a molecular formula of C₆H₁₂O₆)
parole.testo: Borrowed from English glycose, from Ancient Greek γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”). The -óz ending is referring to sugar.
Borrowed from English graphology, from Ancient Greek γράφω (gráphō, “to write”). With -lógia ending.

parole.significato: hormone (any substance produced by one tissue and conveyed by the bloodstream to another to effect physiological activi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from English hormone, from Ancient Greek ὁρμῶν (hormôn), present participle of ὁρμάω (hormáō, “to set in motion, urge on”). Coined by Ernest Starling, British physiologist.
From English ion, from Ancient Greek ἰόν (ión, “going”).
From English isostasy, from Ancient Greek ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + στάσις (stásis, “a standing”).

parole.significato: catheter (a small tube inserted into a body cavity to administer a drug, create an opening, distend a passageway, or re…
parole.testo: From English catheter, from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr).
From English chromosome, ultimately from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour”) + σῶμα (sôma, “body”) (because they are stained under the microscope). See kromo- (“chromo-”).
Borrowed from English microscope, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + σκοπεῖν (skopeîn, “to look at”).

parole.significato: polyhistor (someone gifted or learned in multiple disciplines)
parole.testo: Borrowed from English polyhistor, from Ancient Greek πολυί̈στωρ (poluí̈stōr, “greatly learned”).

parole.significato: stereoscope (instrument used for viewing pairs of stereoscopic photographs)
parole.testo: From English stereoscope, from Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, “solid”) + σκοπεῖν (skopeîn, “to look at”).
From English technology, from Ancient Greek τέχνη (tékhnē, “art”) + -λογία (-logía). With -lógia ending.
